content.title: Applied Machine Learning in Energy Data
content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation

content.text:
This section is an introduction to the role of Machine Learning (ML) in energy policy, with a focus on structured data, supervised and unsupervised learning, and ethical considerations. It explains how ML models are trained using labeled data and test/train splits and how these models can support evidence-based policymaking in areas like energy access, consumption forecasting, and environmental impact.
The lesson moves from foundational ML concepts to specific applications, such as using Random Forests for solar energy 💬️ prediction and clustering for industrial emissions profiling. It concludes by exploring the limitations and ethical concerns tied to ML in public policy, including data bias, transparency, privacy, and explainability, and highlights best practices such as Privacy by Design, Explainable AI, and regulatory sandboxes.

content.title: Machine Learning
content.body: Machine Learning, as commonly defined by Google for Developers, stands for “is the process of training a piece of software, called a model, to make useful predictions or generate content (such as texts, images, audio, or video files) from data.”. More specifically, models that can generate texts, images, audio or video are commonly referred to as Generative AI models, or Gen-AI models. Traditional/conventional ML models attempt to predict values of a variables of interest (a process called regression), or predict a certain class belonging (a process called classification) based on attributes in the data (called features).

content.title: Data Types
content.body: Machine Learning models are typically trained on data. Data formats on which such models are trained fall under two broad categories; Structured Data, which refers to data that is organized, can be filtered and sorted through, as well as unstructured data, such as images, texts, audio files.

content.title: Supervised Learning
content.body: Supervised learning models try to understand the relationship between predictor variables and a variable of interest, the outcome the be predicted. When training an ML model, the available data is subdivided into a training set (where the model parameters are estimated through predictive error), and a test set, where the model is evaluated on data it has not seen. (This is called the train/test split).

content.title: Labeled Datasets
content.body: For classification tasks, where observations are placed in classes/categories based on specific attributes, a dataset with the actual classifications are labeled according to their actual class belonging. Such a set is called a labeled set, which can be structured, unstructured, and must be divided into training and test sets.

content.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
content.body: When training ML models on training and test data, data scientists make sure that the model is not overly complex, and too closely fit to the data (which is called overfitting), and that the model is not too simplistic as to consistently mis-predict the variable of interest (called underfitting), this balance in the model follows a principle called the bias variance tradeoff.

content.title: B: Supervised and Unsupervised Learning for Energy
Tree Based Algorithms
content.body: A popular example of supervised learning algorithms are tree-based algorithms such as classification trees (also known as decision trees) and regression trees. Tree based algorithms work by splitting features into regions and making predictions for region of the feature space, as visualized below.

content.title: Tree Based Algorithms for Energy
content.body: Within the realm of energy policy both decision and regression trees have been used to informed evidence-based policy. One such scenario was in Kenya, where, by taking into account length of Medium Voltage Lines, Low Voltage Lines, Distribution Capacity, Substation Capacity as well as the total number of consumers, researchers are able to estimate the cost of a project. content.title: Random Forests for Energy Consumption
content.body: Through the use of a Random Forest algorithm, Ahmad, Reynolds, and Rezgui (2018) are able to predict hourly useful solar thermal energy for a solar thermal plant in Chambéry, France. Using Solar irradiance, Ambient temperature, Inlet and outlet fluid temperatures to the solar thermal plant, flow rate of the heat transfer fluid, as well as time-related variables, predictions are made. The increased investment and interest in the use of modern ML techniques in the prediction of renewable energy projects allows for effective planning, more grid stability and a more informed path to the sustainable integration of renewable energy sources into the energy mix.

content.title: ML for Academia
content.body: As such, the use of ML models for energy consumption forecasting has captivated the scientific community, with some researchers using it in tandem with classical econometric models (Nie et.al, 2021) or as an alternative to purely statistical models (Tso et.al, 2007).

content.title: Principal Component Analysis and K-means Clustering
content.body: As previously mentioned, unsupervised learning attempt to understand the underlying structure of that data, as opposed to attempting to predict outcomes. This type of understanding has found its way into modern energy policymaking. Two mainstream unsupervised ML algorithms that make their way into the literature are k-means clustering and Principal Component Analysis algorithms.

content.title: Unsupervised Learning Applications
content.body: A further area in which ML models have seen an increased usage is the estimation and classification of households with informal access to energy. Informal access to energy refers to energy that does not come from the national grid, informal access to energy covers sources such as biomass, household generators, unregulated solar energy. Such energy access is usually more expensive and less reliable. Being able to estimate and classify households with informal access goes a long way into helping government better target underdeveloped areas through electrification programs, provide a better return per dollar spent, while also providing policymakers with a clear picture on which communities may be struggling.

content.title: Clustering for Energy
content.body: Clustering aims to group observations into multiple groups- or clusters- by minimizing the squared sum of the distances of each cluster member to the cluster center. This allows analysts to group observations based on their features. In terms of energy policy, Liu et.al (2018) studied 15129 companies listed on the SSE and SZSE stock markets. By analyzing water and coal consumption both between industries and within industries and clustering them into high, low, and medium usage companies, Liu et. al were able to pinpoint highly polluting fields such as chemical production, heat and power generation as opposed to counterintuitively low emitters such as the textile industry and non-ferrous metals. Such studies allow policymakers to benchmark industries, allowing for better long-term planning.

content.title: PCA
content.body: Principal Component Analysis, on the other hand, focus on dimensionality reduction, and thus representing a high dimensional space (or a high number of features), with a smaller, representative one. Within the realm of energy, this allows for a reduction of computational costs, by reducing the size of a dataset, and thus the computational load. In addition, PCA allows for visualization of complex dynamics in a 2D or 3D dimensional space, all while maintaining the important structures.

content.title: PCA for Energy
content.body: · Principal Component Analysis, can also be used to allocate weights based on data as opposed to subjective weights in indices, provided a more objective method of assessment. A simple case example comes from Al Albsahi et. al ‘s work on the Energy Trilemma Index, an index that uses 13 metrics related to energy security, energy equity, and environmental sustainability to rank nations according to their ETI. The weights accorded to the energy security, energy equity and environmental sustainability sections, although provided by experts, remain subjective. By applying PCA to the 13 metrics into one index, these researchers are able to find the allocation of weights that best explains the data. As such, they come to conclusions that differ from the traditional ETI evaluation, ranking Norway as the top country in their revised index as opposed to Switzerland. This has numerous implications with regards to energy policy, shifting away from subjective rating towards more evidence-based estimations.

content.title: D: Limits and Ethics of ML for Energy
Introduction
content.body: Although the use of ML in energy policymaking and energy data in general has benefitted the larger community, while also allowing for better monitoring and more streamlined management, key ethical concerns arise when it comes to the affected populations, their right to privacy, and the implications of using AI in policy contexts.

content.title: Data Representativeness
content.body: A key issue in ML for policy is the representativeness of data, in a sense, how well it generalizes to broader contexts. An intuitive example that comes to mind is a machine learning algorithm trained on historical data from affluent areas. This scenario presents several issues based on various scenarios. For example, in pricing, an ML algorithm trained on affluent area data may not generalize well into worse off areas. This is mainly backed by the essential realization that energy poor areas and areas that have access to energy have fundamentally different usage patterns. A simple way to visualize it is in the use of smart appliances. Whereas affluent households may have access to such technologies that reduce usage in peak hours, less affluent households may not have access to such equipment and bear the brunt by paying peak prices, perpetuating unequal access to affordable energy.

content.title: Privacy, Explainability and Ethical ML
content.body: Additional ethical concerns when applying ML to energy policy are both the sensitivity of the information being gathered, as well as how it is being used. A simple way to think of this is when it comes to smart meters, depending on the granularity of the data collected, it could divulge personal patterns, such as when the subject is home, when they perform various activities. In addition, ethical concerns are raised when data is collected from individuals and used to train algorithms they cannot understand, such as the inner workings of neural networks. These concepts have given rise to the fields of ethics by design (EbD), privacy by design (PbD) and explainable AI (XAI). PbD incorporates built-in privacy safeguards without compromising functionality through measures such as anonymization and the collection of minimal data. EdB incorporates principles of informed consent, data ownership and inclusivity into their design philosophy. Finally, XAI allows citizens to understand which variables affect model predictions most, even when models are complex, an example is the inclusion of SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) measures, which showcase the contribution of specifics features to predictions.

content.title: Future Endeavors
content.body: Ongoing global efforts in terms of data policy privacies regulating cross-border data flows, and a global effort to standardize data access procedures are paving the way for fairer use of data in applications aiming to enhance equitable access to energy.

takeaways.title: ML enables smarter energy planning through both prediction and pattern recognition
takeaways.description: Supervised learning methods like decision trees and Random Forests are effective for forecasting energy production or estimating infrastructure costs. Unsupervised techniques like clustering and PCA help identify hidden patterns, such as informal energy access or industrial pollution profiles, providing policymakers with deeper insights for targeted interventions.

takeaways.title: Unsupervised ML supports evidence-based policy and index construction
takeaways.description: Techniques like PCA can reduce complexity and bias in energy-related indices by allocating weights based on data instead of expert assumptions. This enables more objective assessments of energy security, equity, and sustainability—offering policymakers new ways to benchmark progress and plan reforms.

takeaways.title: Ethical and governance safeguards are essential in applying ML to public policy
takeaways.description: While ML can increase efficiency and insight, risks related to data privacy, bias, and transparency must be actively managed. Approaches like Ethics by Design, Privacy by Design, and Explainable AI (e.g., SHAP values) are vital to ensure ML systems are accountable, inclusive, and equitable—especially when used in public service delivery.
